Task 1. Katie Chandra is the editor of the magazine.

Morning, Dan. You look very well.
Where's Katie? Hi Iris.
She's not here yet but she texted to say she’s on her way.
So um how was your weekend?
Oh, really terrible actually.
Oh dear. I’m sorry to hear that.
What was so awful about it?
Well, my dog was sick.
Oh no. Um, why was your dog sick?
I don’t know.
It was fine all week and then suddenly at the weekend it became really really sick.
Oh that’s terrible.
Well, I hope your dog gets better soon.
Thanks. How about you?
How was yours?
Well, I don’t mean to gloat, but I had a great weekend, a really wonderful weekend Do you want to know why?
Let me tell you.
I bought a new TV, one of those really really big TVs.
It’s totally amazing it’s like real life.
Wow! That sounds cool.
I would love to have a big TV like that.
Oh, here comes Katie now.
Morning guys. Sorry, I’m a bit late.
Morning Katie. So how was your weekend, Katie?
Ugh, Boring, boring, boring!
Why? Why? Why?
Because I had to work, work, work, Dan!
That's my reward for being the boss I suppose having to work all weekend!
Oh well. Right, now, we've got lots to get through.
So for the June edition of the magazine our main theme will be games and play.
Now, I sent out an email last week asking us all to come up with ideas for topics.
Dan? Well, I was thinking of computer games and learning, you know like games that actually teach you a skill.
There’s one called The Next Mozart It’s like a piano playing game.
My knees is always playing it Yeah, that is a good topic.
I'll definitely accept it for the next edition.
These computer games for learning are really popular.
Right, and what have you got for us, Iris?
Well, I’ve been looking at games that young children play in the playground.
Do you mean like playground games?
Yeah, that’s right, playground games.
I was thinking of looking at some examples, you know like Catch the Dragon and Fingers Out Oh yeah.
Did you say Fingers Out I remember Fingers Out I used to play that all the time when I was at primary school.
What was the first game called again?
The Dragon one, Catch the Dragon Oh right.
Not sure if I ever played that one.
Oh I did.
Definitely. Anyway, this is a great topic, Iris.
So you accept it?
Yep, definitely. Playground games are fun to watch.
Lots and lots of fun to watch So right back to you, Dan.
Any other contributions?
Yes. So something I've been looking at is computer games for animals.
I think it would be nice to contrast human games with, like, games animals play.
Well, it sounds interesting.
What do you mean by computer games for animals exactly?
Well, there’s loads of videos on the Internet.
Darks and cats jumping at moving objects on the computer screen.
It’s really funny.
There’s this one game you can get for computer tablets called Crazy Cats.
It’s brilliant. The cat chases a red dot around the screen.
Dan, you're not getting paid to look at funny videos on the Internet.
What research have you done?
Really. Crazy Cat Um, no research.
Sorry. Will you accept my topic though?
Dan you haven't done any research so it’s a no.
I can’t accept topics that haven’t been researched.
Yeah, OK.
That is the end of Task 1.
You now have one minute to tidy tidy up your answers.
Task 2. Iris is working on an online game for the next issue of the magazine.

In Part A, Iris explains the game to Dan.
In Part B, Dan plays the game.
In Part C, Dan and Iris discuss the game.

Part A. Fill in the missing information in the spaces provided in the Monster Maze Key.
Hey Iris. What are you working on?
Well, for this edition of the magazine, I’m designing some games.
You know so that our a subscribers can play them on their phone.
The idea is that they pay money to play and they can win money if they win.
Cool! What kind of games?
Well, the one I’m working on just now is called Monster Maze Have a look.
That’s the key.
I'm just finishing the example for the Key just now.
Hmm. The grid looks good.
OK, good. So where’s the entrance to the maze?
Is it at the top here?
No, the other way round.
The entrance to the maze is at the bottom where the numbers 1 to 6 are.
Ah I see, where the numbers are.
So the exit to the maze is at the top then.
Exactly. The exit at the top.
Oh, OK. Right.
And the grey squares must be walls or something.
Yes, that’s right, the grey squares are the walls of the maze.
And those circles, the Os.
That indicates the root you have taken through the maze.
Oh, I see the o's.
And what’s this M here?
That's the monster.
There are three but they're hidden when you play the game but when you land on one of the monsters an M appears and you lose a life.
Right. Still not sure if I get it.
So have a look at the example in the Key.
OK. Well, in the example, the player starts on A4, goes forward one square to B4, moves left one square to B3, moves forward three squares to E3
and then moves left one square and there at E2 he lands on the monster.
And is dead.
Yep. Yep. Eden alive.
Exactly.
Be. Plot Dan’s root by putting a circle in each square like the example shown above in the Monster Maze Key and put an M if he lands on a hidden monster.
So, do you want to play, Dan?
Sure. OK we can do it without the computer just now.
now. So I'll hide three monsters on the grid by writing down the grid number, and you have to go from the entrance of the maze and reach the exit without walking into the monsters.
You get two lives.
Sure. So this is my first life eh?
Yeah. Come on.
Go! OK, OK, I’m thinking.
I'll start on A4.
OK. You're fine.
Next move. I'll move forward one square then.
move right two squares.
gotcha You've landed on my monster.
ah Okay, so Your second life.
Right my second life.
Here goes. I'll start at a5 I move forward one square.
Now, I'll move left two squares.
OK. You're fine.
Move forward three squares.
And move right one square.
OK. Here it goes Move forward one square.
Did I make it?
Yes, well done Dan, you made it!
You survived the maze.
Hooray! I won.
No longer will I be We caught a loser!
Well, I don’t know about that!
Part C. Listen to Iris and Dan’s discussion and answer the questions.
Please note you do not have to answer in full sentences.
So, what do you think?
Any suggestions? Hmm.
Well, the grid’s a bit boring to look at.
You need to make the game look more colourful.
Yes, it does look a bit boring you're right.
I'll ask Gabby in graphics to make it more colourful.
And I'd suggest having more monsters.
that'll make it more challenging.
Yes, I suppose adding more monsters would make it more fun too.
But I have a question.
I was just wondering how will people actually play it online?
The game, I mean.
Well, we're going to allow two ways of playing the game.
The first one is by actually speaking, like we did.
Oh, that’s quite cool, so you speak to your smartphone and it marks your root on the grid.
Yes, that’s right.
All voice controlled.
The second way is that you can simply touch the screen.
Yes. I can imagine this working well with like touchscreen devices like smartphones.
But how can people be sure that the game’s not cheating and, you know, just placing the the monsters up to the player makes a move?
This is the tricky part.
It’s done in steps.
So in the first step, when the game starts, the game sends a document to the player’s phone.
OK, so what happens up to that?
Right, the second step is that when the game's over, a password appears on the screen, OK, right.
And then? What's the password for?
Right, so the third step is that the player opens the document with the password.
OK, cool. So they open the document in the third step.
Then the fourth and final step is that the player checks the location of the monsters.
OK, that is clever.
So when the player checks the location, he knows then that the game hasn’t been cheating.
Exactly.
That is the end of Task 2.
You now have one minute to tidy up your answers.
Task 3 Katie is at the airport.
She is calling Dan to ask him to edit an article she has been working on.
There are three parts to Task 3.
In Part A, you have to correct some sentences.
In Part B, you have to provide labels for parts of a painting and in Part C you have to complete a text.

Part A. Each line of the text below may have one mistake.
Correct the mistake as shown below.
If the line is correct then put a tick in the right hand column.

Hello. Oh hi Dan.
Hi, where are you?
I'm at the airport.
Look Dan. I’ve written this article about games and art but didn’t have time to finish editing it, and like an idiot, I forgot my laptop.
I need you to check some things for me.

Can you change it?
OK. Done. Okay.
OK, now can you double check some of the facts are written correctly?
I might have got the dates wrong.

No, no. It’s right.
You say here that it was started in 1560.
Ah, just as well you said that.
It was completed then.

Oh you’ve actually written Pete Bruegel, P -E -T -E.
Oh, Thought so.
OK let me just change that now.
OK. Right, and make sure I’ve got the countries right.
I can never remember where he was born and died.
He died in Belgium and was born in the Netherlands.
Got it? Yeah I think so.
Part B. Label the four games the children are playing in the painting.
Use no more than four words for each.
OK, now the next thing is that I’ve put some labels on the painting to point out interesting details about what the children are actually doing the games they’re playing, I mean.
I didn’t manage to finish them.
Could you add them as I go through them?
Yes, let’s see.
I've got the picture up here now.
So, if you look closely, there’s one boy sitting cross legged on the grass.
Well, this was actually a form of exercise at the time, a bit like yoga today.
OK, I can see that now.
It does look like he’s doing a yoga exercise.
I didn’t realize before.
Also, in the picture, there are girls holding a basket.
Oh yes. I see them.
Seems to be a basket of fruit or something.
So what are they doing then?
It doesn’t look like a game.
Well, they’re actually performing a wedding.
A pretend wedding.
Oh, I remember having to dress up for pretend weddings when I was little with my big sister.
Oh, now that would be a wedding picture I'd love to see!
Yeah, well. Now, what else?
OK, you see those boys on top of the fence?
Well, they’re playing at riding horses.
Oh yes. I can see that now.
They really do look like they are riding a horse.
course. So what about the kids jumping over the other kid’s legs.
What’s that about?
This game's actually quite painful.
The children would apparently kick very hard and it would really hurt.
Ouch! So it’s a kicking game!
I’m glad we didn’t play that when I was at school.
We did something similar actually.
Kicking people I mean.
It was quite violent.
Part C. Complete the text.
Write one or more words in each gap.
Right, moving on.
What else is there?
Oh yes, at the end of the article there’s a section on present day games.
Games that use classic art for their graphics.
I didn’t quite finish that.
Oh, OK. They look fun.
Yeah, I loved reading up on this.
I like the fact that they're making a video game out of a classic work of art like The Last Supper or The Mona Lisa.
Yeah, I know.
They’re brilliant aren't they.
So what’s interesting is that these games use 8 -bit graphics.
8 bit? You mean like early computer graphics?
Why is 8 -bit graphics?
That’s a bit weird.
Well, because for the game designers it’s a challenge.
They’re trying to use these little blocks with only a few colours to create very complex pictures.
Hmm. What I mean is that they, the designers of these computer games, enjoy making these really complicated images from small blocks using only a small number of colours.
Yeah, OK. Well, Let me just finish making a note of that.
Right, keep going.
So the games themselves are actually quite simple, like really really simple and there’s a reason for that.
And what's the reason?
Well, these games are not meant to be serious.
They’re just supposed to be funny.
You mean humorous funny?
Not weird funny?
Yeah exactly. Like a joke.
And where can you find these games?
Do you have to pay for them?
You can get them on the Internet.
The good thing is they’re free.
You don’t need to pay anything.
Free. Well, that makes a change.
Maybe I'll check them out.
Is that everything?
Yes, that’s all.
Thanks for helping out, Dan.
That is the end of Task 3.
You now have one minute to tidy up your answers.
Task 4. You will listen to the What, Why, How weekly podcast.
Katie is discussing the psychology of games and play with two professors of psychology.
Answer the questions below and complete the table.
You now have 30 seconds to study the task.
task. At the end of the task, you will have three minutes to tidy up your answers.
Hi well, today I’m joined by Dr Jonathan Newman from the University of Jung Yee An.
Good morning. And Dr Natalie Sum from the University of Eastern Australia.
Good morning Katie.
Our discussion today is about the psychology of games and play.
So let’s dive in, shall Are we?
Can we define what a game is first of all?
Jonathan? Help! That’s a challenge.
Well, we may say that most games have at least two key aspects in common.
First, they provide some form of entertainment.
We seek out games primarily for pleasure and fun.
The second thing is that they seem to have some outcome or goal.
goal. For instance, you either win or lose a game or finish it in some way.
Would you agree with that Natalie?
Yes, Jonathan. Well, it’s certainly true that games are primarily for entertainment and that games all have some kind of outcome.
I would like to add a third aspect.
Would you agree with me that games must follow some set of rules too?
Yes, I’d agree that following rules would be an essential element of games in general.
You know, Jonathan, to me what’s most fascinating is how games and life are so similar.
I’d even say life itself is but a game.
Life is a game?
I hope you don’t actually mean that.
But it is, is it not?
Life is simply a game we all have to play.
Maybe your life’s a game Natalie.
Mine isn’t and I don’t think anyone else’s is either.
Actually, not even yours.
Oh, Jonathan, your problem is you need to get some more fun in life, I mean OK, let’s leave that point there.
Now, both of you have done a great deal of research into games and play in animals.
Would you like to give some examples?
Sure. Well, here’s something that'll surprise you.
Do you know ants play fight?
No. Really?
Ants! It’s really true.
That's incredible so they actually get better at real fighting from play fighting.
Here’s another one that gets me.
Fish play. You know sometimes when you're watching fish in a pond and they suddenly jump out for no apparent reason?
Yeah, I’ve seen that.
I thought they'd jump to catch food.
No, no they'd jump for the fun of it.
Most fish feed underwater.
water, But this play jumping helps them in certain situations like if they have to escape something trying to eat them.
Yes, apparently jumping helps them escape from predators and hunters.
But to me what's really fascinating is how playing games actually develop morality in all kinds of animals.
Can you give an example?
Well, rats often engage in play fighting games.
There are three points to note here.
First, play fighting games occur between stronger and weaker rats.
So one rat will always be stronger than another rat?
Precisely. I mean the same is true in any kind of game.
Someone will always be a bit better or a bit worse than the other player.
Now, the second point is where it It's interesting.
If the weaker rat always loses, it will stop playing.
You mean the weaker rat says, Right, I'm not playing this game if you keep winning.
That’s how I feel when I play scrabble or chess with my daughter!
Now for the third and most interesting part.
The stronger rat learns that it has to let the weaker rat win some of the time so they can keep playing.
Oh! So, the stronger rat will deliberately lose to the weaker rat, otherwise it'll have no friends to play with.
Oh, Poor strong rat with no friends.
So I guess they are learning something very important from this Absolutely.
For one thing, they are developing a kind of morality.
The second thing is that they learn how to live together peacefully.
Wow, Wow! That's amazing.
So rats have to learn to be moral and they have to learn how to live peacefully with one another, just like us humans have to do.
That’s absolutely fascinating.
OK, well, we're going to have a short break and when we come back Natalie and Jonathan will be answering some of your questions.
That is the end of Task 4 and of Part 3A.
You now have three minutes to complete your answers to Task 4 and to tidy up all your other answers.

Situation You are Sami Tsung.
You work for a board game company called Griffin Workshop in Hong Kong.
It is a small company set up by some friends.
It is now working on its latest board game Escape to Hong Kong Island.
Your boss, Angel Fu, has asked you to do some tasks.

Hi there listeners and welcome to today’s edition of The Classical.
I'm your host David Choi and today’s program focuses on board gaming.
I have two people with me in the studio today to help discuss this and they are firstly Angel Fu.
Hello David. who is a local board game producer, that’s right isn’t it?
That's right David.
And also Eric Park, who is a well -known board game designer from California California in the USA.
Hi David, glad to be in Hong Kong.
So, Angel. I understand that you've started your own local board game company.
That's right. And what's the name of your company?
Griffin Workshop. So why did you decide to start your company?
Well, we’re four friends and we I mean, all four of us we really wanted to make our own board games.
So that was why you started then because you wanted to make your own board games?
Yes and we thought why not start a games company.
And so there are four of you?
That's right. Oh wait a minute, there's actually five members of the company.
We recently employed a new person, Sammy's dung.
If you're listening, hi Sammy!
So you're all from Hong Kong?
Yes, that’s right.
Hong Kong born and bred.
Well it’s nice to see a local company.
When did you form the company?
Two years ago in 2016.
OK, so quite a new company.
So Eric, Angel's company just started out.
They have an idea for a game.
They want to move ahead.
What advice would you give her and her company?
Well, supposing that you have developed a game, Yes, yes we have.
Right well, the next stage is obviously that you need to decide how to get funds to make your game.
Ah, of course.
Money. Yes, well, a small company needs to get funds to produce the game because producing the game can be quite expensive.
And I personally think that the best way to get funds is through Game Start.
Oh, OK. And what is Game Start?
Well, Game Start is the most well -known funding website for board game companies.
Right. So what's the main advantage of using Game Start as a source of funds then?
Well, I'd say the main advantage of something like Game Start is it’s global so Because it’s online.
Exactly, so you can get money from investors from, well basically, anywhere in the world.
OK, well, that sounds the way to go.
Yeah, Yeah, but don’t forget there are other ways besides Game Start to get funding.
Such as? Like, getting a grant from a local company.
OK. I mean, there are local grants available where you can win money as an award.
In Hong Kong, one of the best known of these is the Acorn Grant.
You might have heard of it.
Yeah, actually we’ve been looking into applying for the Acorn Grant.
Good, though with a grant like the ACON Grant there are definitely disadvantages.
Like what? Well often when you get a grant they tell you that they'll give you lots of help but really they just want to control everything.
The ACON Grant has the reputation for being one of those.
Really? Yeah, I’m afraid so.
Oh I don’t want that.
Me and my friends at Griffin Workshop just want to be independent.
We We don’t really want other people to control us.
Well, if you value your independence, then a grant like the ACON Grant maybe isn’t your best option.
OK, now Angel, back to the games that Griffin Workshop make.
Have you actually made any games yet?
Yeah, we've made two games.
We've published the first one and we are now working on the second one.
So tell us about the first one.
OK, our first game was called Death Kick.
Death Kick! Now that is a good name.
And it’s a card game.
A card game?
And from the sound of it, it’s a fighting game, I’m guessing.
Yeah. It’s a Kung Fu card game.
A Kung Fu card game!
Yeah, I've played Death Kick and I thought it was really good.
Oh wow! OK, well, tell us about your second game.
game. The latest one.
OK. Our latest game is called Escape to Hong Kong Island and is it a zombie game.
A zombie game, OK.
Is it set in Hong Kong?
Yes that’s right, set in Hong Kong.
OK, so what happens in the game?
Right well, the players start in Kowloon and OK, they’re in Kowloon.
Yes, and the players have to reach Hong Kong Island.
And so the first player who gets to Hong Kong Island is the winner.
Actually no. It’s a team game, so everybody in your team has to reach Hong Kong Island.
So if everybody in your team reaches Hong Kong Island, your team is the winner?
Is that the idea?
That's right. If all your team members manage to get to Hong Kong Island, that’s it you've won.
Sounds good. So Eric.
As an experienced game designer, designer.
what advice would you give Angel about Escape to Hong Kong Island?
Well, it sounds pretty interesting.
I would say that the first thing you need to do is be very clear who your target audience is.
Who’s your target audience for the game, Angel?
Young teenagers. OK.
Well, a word of warning then, young teenagers is often the trickiest age group to sell a game to.
And has your artist designed some of the artwork yet?
Yes. We have samples of artwork.
Well OK, one thing to always remember, if your audience is young teenagers, is that parents usually have the final say in whether the game gets bought or not.
Oh, OK. I mean, either parents themselves buy it for their kids for something like a birthday present or they’ll demand to see what their son or daughter has bought.
Oh. Very often you have to remind your artist about this.
Sometimes an artist will often get carried away and they'll produce this beautiful work, and that may well appeal to the young teenager, but the parents won’t approve because it’s just too graphic.
And by graphic you mean?
Too adult. Art that’s just too violent usually.
apparently. Parents won't buy or won't let their kids buy it.
Well, that’s some pretty sound advice for you there, Angel.
OK, I think we're out of time now and I'd like to thank you both for coming in to chat to us today.
That is the end of the listening component of this paper.
You will now have one hour and 15 minutes to complete the written tasks in either Part B1 or Part B2.
An announcement will be made when time is up.
Take off your earphones now and turn off the radio.
